section.heading: 16.4. Green’s Theorem
section.paragraph: Green’s Theorem gives the relationship between a line integral around a simple closed curve and a double integral over the plane region bounded by the curve.
section.heading: Green’s Theorem
section.paragraph: Let $$C$$ be a simple closed curve and let $$D$$ be the region bounded by $$C$$ , as in Figure 1. (We assume that $$D$$ consists of all points inside $$C$$ as well as all points on $$C$$ .) In stating Green’s Theorem we use the convention that the positive orientation of a simple closed curve $$C$$ refers to a single counterclockwise traversal of $$C$$ . Thus if $$C$$ is given by the vector function $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ , $$a \leqslant t \leqslant b$$ , then the region $$D$$ is always on the left as the point $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ traverses $$C$$ . (See Figure 2.)

note.title: Green’s Theorem
note.heading: Green’s Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$C$$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane and let $$D$$ be the region bounded by $$C$$ . If $$P$$ and $$Q$$ have continuous partial derivatives on an open region that contains $$D$$ , then
$$\int_{C}Pdx + Qdy = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}}$$

section.paragraph: Recall that the left side of this equation is another way of writing $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ , where $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}$$ .
Note The notation
$$\oint_{C}{Pdx + Qdy}$$
or
$$\oint_{C}{Pdx + Qdy}$$

is sometimes used to indicate that the line integral is calculated using the positive orientation of the closed curve $$C$$ . Another notation for the positively oriented boundary curve of $$D$$ is $$\partial D$$ , so the equation in Green’s Theorem can be written as
$$\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA = {\int_{\partial D}{Pdx + Qdy}}}$$

Green’s Theorem should be regarded as the counterpart of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for double integrals. Compare Equation 1 with the statement of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2, in the following equation:
$$\int_{a}^{b}{F^{\prime}(x)dx = F(b) - F(a)}$$

In both cases there is an integral involving derivatives ( $$F^{\prime}$$ , $$\partial Q \slash \partial x$$ , and $$\partial P \slash \partial y$$ ) on the left side of the equation. And in both cases the right side involves the values of the original functions ( $$F$$ , $$Q$$ , and $$P$$ ) only on the boundary of the domain. (In the one-dimensional case, the domain is an interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ whose boundary consists of just two points, $$a$$ and $$b$$ .)
Green’s Theorem is not easy to prove in general, but we can give a proof for the special case where the region is both type I and type II (see Section 15.2). Let’s call such regions simple regions.

note.source_type: Proof of Green’s Theorem for the Case in Which D Is a Simple Region
note.title: Proof of Green’s Theorem for the Case in Which D Is a Simple Region
note.heading: Proof of Green’s Theorem for the Case in Which D Is a Simple Region
note.paragraph: Notice that Green’s Theorem will be proved if we can show that
$$\int_{C}{Pdx = - {\iint\limits_{D}{\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}dA}}}$$
and
$$\int_{C}{Qdy = {\iint\limits_{D}{\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}dA}}}$$
We prove Equation 2 by expressing $$D$$ as a type I region:
$$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| a \leqslant x \leqslant b,g_{1}(x) \leqslant y \leqslant g_{2}(x) \right\}$$
where $$g_{1}$$ and $$g_{2}$$ are continuous functions. This enables us to compute the double integral on the right side of Equation 2 as follows:

$${\iint\limits_{D}{\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}dA = {\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{g_{1}(x)}^{g_{2}(x)}{\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}}}} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {P\left( {x,g_{2}(x)} \right) - P\left( {x,g_{1}(x)} \right)} \right\rbrack dx}}$$
where the last step follows from the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

Now we compute the left side of Equation 2 by breaking up $$C$$ as the union of the four curves $$C_{1}$$ , $$C_{2}$$ , $$C_{3}$$ , and $$C_{4}$$ shown in Figure 3. On $$C_{1}$$ we take $$x$$ as the parameter and write the parametric equations as $$x = x$$ , $$y = g_{1}(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . Thus
$$\int_{C_{1}}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx = {\int_{a}^{b}{P\left( {x,g_{1}(x)} \right)dx}}}$$

Observe that $$C_{3}$$ goes from right to left but $$- C_{3}$$ goes from left to right, so we can write the parametric equations of $$- C_{3}$$ as $$x = x$$ , $$y = g_{2}(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . Therefore
$$\int_{C_{3}}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx = - {\int_{- C_{3}}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx = - {\int_{a}^{b}{P\left( {x,g_{2}(x)} \right)dx}}}}}$$
On $$C_{2}$$ or $$C_{4}$$ (either of which might reduce to just a single point), $$x$$ is constant, so $$dx = 0$$ and
$$\int_{C_{2}}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx = 0 = {\int_{C_{4}}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx}}}$$
Hence

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{C}P(x,y)dx} = {\int_{C_{1}}P(x,y)dx + \int_{C_{2}}P(x,y)dx + \int_{C_{3}}P(x,y)dx + \int_{C_{4}}P(x,y)dx}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}P(x,y)dx} = {\int_{a}^{b}P\left( {x,g_{1}(x)} \right)dx - \int_{a}^{b}P\left( {x,g_{2}(x)} \right)dx}} \end{array}$$
Comparing this expression with the one in Equation 4, we see that
$$\int_{C}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx = - {\iint\limits_{D}{\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}dA}}}$$
Equation 3 can be proved in much the same way by expressing $$D$$ as a type II region (see Exercise 34). Then, by adding Equations 2 and 3, we obtain Green’s Theorem.

image.alt: Details A four-part closed curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x-axis has two tick marks: a and b, with a to the left of b. The first curve, labeled C_1, defined by y = g_1(x), begins from directly above a, briefly goes down to the right, concaves up, reaches a low point, and then goes up to the right, concaves down until directly above b. The region within the four-part closed curve is labeled D.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\int_{C}{x^{4}dx + xydy}}_{}$$ , where $$C$$ is the triangular curve consisting of the line segments from $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ , from $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ , and from $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ .

Solution Although the given line integral could be evaluated as usual by the methods of Section 16.2, that would involve setting up three separate integrals along the three sides of the triangle, so let’s use Green’s Theorem instead. Notice that the region $$D$$ enclosed by $$C$$ is simple and $$C$$ has positive orientation (see Figure 4). If we let $$P\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{4}$$ and $$Q\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ , then we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{C}x^{4}dx + xydy = \iint\limits_{D}\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA} = {\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1 - x}(y - 0)dydx}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}x^{4}dx + xydy} = {\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}y^{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 1 - x}dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}{(1 - x)}^{2}dx}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}x^{4}dx + xydy}{= - \frac{1}{6}{(1 - x)}^{3}\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{6}}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A triangular curve and a shaded region are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The triangular curve has its vertices at (0, 0), (1, 0), and (0, 1). An arrowhead is placed on each side of the triangle and points counterclockwise. The hypotenuse of the triangle is labeled y = 1 minus x). The region within the curve is shaded and labeled D.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\oint_{C}{{({3y - e^{\sin x}})}dx}} + \left( {7x + \sqrt{y^{4} + 1}} \right)dy$$ , where $$C$$ is the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$$ .
Solution The region $$D$$ bounded by $$C$$ is the disk $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 9$$ , so let’s change to polar coordinates after applying Green’s Theorem:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\oint_{C}{(3y - e^{\sin x})}^{}dx} + {\left( {7x + \sqrt{y^{4} + 1}} \right)dy} = {\iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {7x + \sqrt{y^{4} + 1}} \right) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}{({3y - e^{\sin x}})}} \right\rbrack dA}} \\ {\phantom{{\oint_{C}{(3y - e^{\sin x})}^{}dx} + {{({7x + \sqrt{y^{4} + 1}})}dy}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{3}(7 - 3)rdrd\theta = 4\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\int_{0}^{3}rdr = 36\pi}} \end{array}$$
Instead of using polar coordinates, we could simply use the fact that $$D$$ is a disk of radius $$3$$ and write
$$\iint\limits_{D}4dA = 4 \cdot \pi(3)^{2} = 36\pi$$

section.paragraph: In Examples 1 and 2 we found that the double integral was easier to evaluate than the line integral. (Try setting up the line integral in Example 2 and you’ll soon be convinced!) But sometimes it’s easier to evaluate the line integral, and Green’s Theorem is used in the reverse direction. For instance, if it is known that $$P\left( {x,y} \right) = Q\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ on the curve $$C$$ , then Green’s Theorem gives
$$\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA = {\int_{C}{Pdx + Qdy = 0}}}$$
no matter what values $$P$$ and $$Q$$ assume in the region $$D$$ .
section.heading: Finding Areas with Green's Theorem
section.paragraph: Another application of the reverse direction of Green’s Theorem is in computing areas. Since the area of $$D$$ is $$\iint_{D}{1dA}$$ , we wish to choose $$P$$ and $$Q$$ so that
$$\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1$$
There are several possibilities:
$$\begin{array}{lll} {P(x,y) = 0} & { P(x,y) = - y} & { P(x,y) = - \frac{1}{2}y} \\ {Q(x,y) = x} & { Q(x,y) = 0} & { Q(x,y) = \frac{1}{2}x} \end{array}$$
Then Green’s Theorem gives the following formulas for the area of $$D$$ :
$$A = {\oint_{C}{xdy = - {\oint_{C}{ydx = \frac{1}{2}{\oint_{C}{xdy - ydx}}}}}}$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the area enclosed by the ellipse $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$ .
Solution The ellipse has parametric equations $$x = a\cos t$$ and $$y = b\sin t$$ , where $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Using the third formula in Equation 5, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\frac{1}{2}\int_{C}xdy - ydx}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}(a\cos t)(b\cos t)dt - (b\sin t)( - a\sin t)dt}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\frac{ab}{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}dt = \pi ab}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Formula 5 can be used to explain how planimeters work. A planimeter is an ingenious mechanical instrument invented in the 19th century for measuring the area of a region by tracing its boundary curve. For instance, a biologist could use one of these devices to measure the surface area of a leaf or bird wing.

Figure 5 shows the operation of a polar planimeter: the pole is fixed and, as the tracer is moved along the boundary curve of the region, the wheel partly slides and partly rolls perpendicular to the tracer arm. The planimeter measures the distance that the wheel rolls and this is proportional to the area of the enclosed region. The explanation as a consequence of Formula 5 can be found in the following articles:

list.item: R. W. Gatterman, “The planimeter as an example of Green’s Theorem” Amer. Math. Monthly, Vol. 88 (1981), pp. 701–4.
Tanya Leise, “As the planimeter wheel turns” College Math. Journal, Vol. 38 (2007), pp. 24–31.

The planimeter has a tracer that touches the curve and is connected to a beam labeled tracer arm on top. The tracer arm is connected to the front right corner of a rectangular frame. The left side of the frame has two wheels touching each other: one rotates left and right and the other rotate front and back. The top right corner of the frame is labeled pivot and is connected to the left end of a rod labeled polearm with a short cylinder labeled pole at its right end.

note.title: George Green
note.heading: George Green
note.paragraph: Green’s Theorem is named after the self-taught English scientist George Green (1793–1841). He worked full-time in his father’s bakery from the age of nine and taught himself mathematics from library books. In 1828 he published privately An Essay on the Application of Mathematical Analysis to the Theories of Electricity and Magnetism, but only $$100$$ copies were printed and most of those went to his friends. This pamphlet contained a theorem that is equivalent to what we know as Green’s Theorem, but it didn’t become widely known at that time. Finally, at age 40, Green entered Cambridge University as an undergraduate but died four years after graduation. In 1846 William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) located a copy of Green’s essay, realized its significan e, and had it reprinted. Green was the first person to try to formulate a mathematical theory of electricity and magnetism. His work was the basis for the subsequent electromagnetic theories of Thomson, Stokes, Rayleigh, and Maxwell.

section.heading: Extended Versions of Green’s Theorem
section.paragraph: Although we have proved Green’s Theorem only for the case where $$D$$ is simple, we can now extend it to the case where $$D$$ is a finite union of simple regions. For example, if $$D$$ is the region shown in Figure 6, then we can write $$D = D_{1} \cup D_{2}$$ , where $$D_{1}$$ and $$D_{2}$$ are both simple. The boundary of $$D_{1}$$ is $$C_{1} \cup C_{3}$$ and the boundary of $$D_{2}$$ is $$C_{2} \cup \left( {- C_{3}} \right)$$ so, applying Green’s Theorem to $$D_{1}$$ and $$D_{2}$$ separately, we get

$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{C_{1} \cup C_{3}}{Pdx}} + {Qdy} = {\iint\limits_{D_{1}}\left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right)dA}} \\ {{\int_{C_{2} \cup ( - C_{3})}{Pdx}} + {Qdy} = {\iint\limits_{D_{2}}\left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right)dA}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A closed curve, two points, and a line segment are displayed. The closed curve resembles a bent rectangle. Imagine a horizontal rectangle with rounded corners bent upward and concave up. Arrowheads are placed on the curve point counterclockwise. A point is marked at the lowest point of the top and bottom sides of the closed curve and the lower one is directly below the upper one. The part of the curve to the left of the points is labeled C_2 and the part of the curve to the right is labeled C_2. A vertical line segment is drawn connecting the two points. A vertical arrow drawn to the left of the line segment points upward and is labeled C_3. Another vertical arrow drawn to the right of the line segment points downward and is labeled negative C_3. The area within the closed curve to the left of the line segment is labeled D_1 and the area to the right of the line segment is labeled D_2.

section.paragraph: If we add these two equations, the line integrals along $$C_{3}$$ and $$- C_{3}$$ cancel, so we get
$$\int_{C_{1} \cup C_{2}}{Pdx + Qdy = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}}}$$
which is Green’s Theorem for $$D = D_{1} \cup D_{2}$$ , since its boundary is $$C = C_{1} \cup C_{2}$$ .
The same sort of argument allows us to establish Green’s Theorem for any finite union of nonoverlapping simple regions (see Figure 7).

The left end of the rectangle turns and is pulled leftward. Arrowheads are placed on the curve point counterclockwise. The second line segment is horizontal and connects the two parts just before the left arm turns. The third line segment is vertical and is drawn near the left end of the closed curve. Each line segment has two arrows drawn near it. The first and third have an arrow pointing upward on the left and a downward pointing arrow on the right. The second horizontal line segment has a leftward pointing arrow above it and a rightward arrow below it.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\oint_{C}{y^{2}dx + 3xydy}$$ , where $$C$$ is the boundary of the semiannular region $$D$$ in the upper half-plane between the circles $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ and $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ .
Solution Notice that although $$D$$ is not simple, the $$y$$ -axis divides it into two simple regions (see Figure 8). In polar coordinates we can write
$$D = \left\{ \left( {r,\theta} \right) \middle| 1 \leqslant r \leqslant 2,0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi \right\}$$
Therefore Green’s Theorem gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\oint_{C}y^{2}dx + 3xydy} = {\iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(3xy) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y^{2})} \right\rbrack^{}dA}} \\ {\phantom{\oint\limits_{C}y^{2}dx + 3xydy} = {\iint\limits_{D}ydA = \int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{1}^{2}(r\sin\theta)rdrd\theta}} \\ {\phantom{\oint\limits_{C}y^{2}dx + 3xydy} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin\theta d\theta\int_{1}^{2}r^{2}dr = \left\lbrack - \cos\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{3}r^{3}} \right\rbrack_{1}^{2} = \frac{14}{3}}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A semiannular region is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The region remains above the x axis, resting on it with its center at the origin. The boundary of the region resembles two concentric semicircles above the x axis, resting on it, with line segments connecting their starting points and endpoints. The inner semicircle is labeled x^2 + y^2 = 1. An arrowhead placed on the inner semicircle points clockwise. A line segment begins from the end of the inner semicircle on the positive x axis, runs horizontally rightward along the positive x axis, and ends at the end of the outer semicircle on the positive x axis. An arrowhead placed on this line segment points rightward. The outer semicircle is labeled x^2 + y^2 = 4. An arrowhead placed on this semicircle points counterclockwise. From the end of the outer semicircle on the negative x axis, a horizontal line segment runs rightward to meet the end of the inner semicircle on the negative x axis. An arrowhead placed on this line segment points rightward.

section.paragraph: Green’s Theorem can be extended to apply to regions with holes, that is, regions that are not simply-connected. Observe that the boundary $$C$$ of the region $$D$$ in Figure 9 consists of two simple closed curves $$C_{1}$$ and $$C_{2}$$ . We assume that these boundary curves are oriented so that the region $$D$$ is always on the left as the curve $$C$$ is traversed. Thus the positive direction is counterclockwise for the outer curve $$C_{1}$$ but clockwise for the inner curve $$C_{2}$$ . If we divide $$D$$ into two regions $$D^{\prime}$$ and $$D^{''}$$ by means of the lines shown in Figure 10 and then apply Green’s Theorem to each of $$D^{\prime}$$ and $$D^{''}$$ , we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}} = {{\iint\limits_{D^{\prime}}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}} + {\iint\limits_{D^{''}}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}} = {\int_{\partial D^{\prime}}Pdx + Qdy + \int_{\partial D^{''}}Pdx + Qdy}} \end{array}$$
Since the line integrals along the common boundary lines are in opposite directions, they cancel and we get
$$\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA = {\int_{C_{1}}{Pdx + Qdy + {\int_{C_{2}}{Pdx + Qdy = {\int_{C}{Pdx + Qdy}}}}}}}$$
which is Green’s Theorem for the region $$D$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y} \right) = \left( {- y\mathbf{i} + x\mathbf{j}} \right) \slash {({x^{2} + y^{2}})}$$ , show that $$\int_{C}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = 2\pi$$ for every positively oriented simple closed path that encloses the origin.

Solution Since $$C$$ is an arbitrary closed path that encloses the origin, it’s difficult to compute the given integral directly. So let’s consider a counterclockwise-oriented circle $$C^{\prime}$$ with center the origin and radius $$a$$ , where $$a$$ is chosen to be small enough that $$C^{\prime}$$ lies inside $$C$$ . (See Figure 11.) Let $$D$$ be the region bounded by $$C$$ and $$C^{\prime}$$ . Then its positively oriented boundary is $$C \cup \left( {- C^{\prime}} \right)$$ and so the general version of Green’s Theorem gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{C}Pdx + Qdy + \int_{- C^{\prime}}Pdx + Qdy} = {{\iint\limits_{D}\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)}dA}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}Pdx + Qdy + \int_{- C^{\prime}}Pdx + Qdy} = {{\iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {\frac{y^{2} - x^{2}}{{(x^{2} + y^{2})}^{2}} - \frac{y^{2} - x^{2}}{{(x^{2} + y^{2})}^{2}}} \right\rbrack}dA = 0}} \end{array}$$
Therefore
$$\int_{C}{Pdx + Qdy = {\int_{C^{\prime}}{Pdx + Qdy}}}$$
that is,
$$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\int_{C^{\prime}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}}}$$
We now easily compute this last integral using the parametrization given by $$\mathbf{r}(t) = a\cos t\mathbf{i} + a\sin t\mathbf{j}$$ , $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Thus

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\mathbf{F}\left( \mathbf{r}(t) \right) \cdot \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)dt}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{F \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {{\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{( - a\sin t)( - a\sin t) + (a\cos t)(a\cos t)}{a^{2}\cos^{2}t + a^{2}\sin^{2}t}}dt = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{dt = 2\pi}}}} \end{array}$$

The first curve, labeled C, almost resembles a rectangle with curved sides and rounded edges, with its right side, bent upward. The curve includes areas from all four quadrants. section.paragraph: We end this section by using Green’s Theorem to discuss a result that was stated in the preceding section.

note.title: Sketch of Proof of Theorem 16.3.6
note.heading: Sketch of Proof of Theorem 16.3.6
note.paragraph: We’re assuming that $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}$$ is a vector field on an open simply-connected region $$D$$ , that $$P$$ and $$Q$$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives, and that
$${\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}} {{throughout}D}$$
If $$C$$ is any simple closed path in $$D$$ and $$R$$ is the region that $$C$$ encloses, then Green’s Theorem gives

$$\oint_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\oint_{C}{Pdx + Qdy = {\iint\limits_{R}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA = {\iint\limits_{R}{0dA = 0}}}}}}}$$

A curve that is not simple crosses itself at one or more points and can be broken up into a number of simple curves. We have shown that the line integrals of $$\mathbf{F}$$ around these simple curves are all $$0$$ and, adding these integrals, we see that $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = 0}$$ for any closed curve $$C$$ . Therefore $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ is independent of path in $$D$$ by Theorem 16.3.3. It follows that $$\mathbf{F}$$ is a conservative vector field.
